convivial.path: Latin convivium meant a feast where people lived it up together, eating and drinking as one company. The adjective kept that banquet-hall warmth: festive, sociable, good company.

convoke.path: Straightforward from Latin: a convoked assembly is one literally called into being by summons, everyone gathered by a single call.

convoluted.path: Something convolutus is coiled like rope wound on itself. A convoluted argument is pictured the same way: folded back on itself so many times a listener cannot trace it straight through.

copious.path: Latin copia (itself co- 'together' + ops 'wealth, power') meant plenty or a large supply. Copious simply keeps that sense of overflowing quantity.

cordial.path: Medieval Latin cordialis meant 'of or from the heart.' A cordial greeting is imagined as coming straight from the heart, sincere and warm rather than merely polite.

cornucopia.path: The mythical goat's horn that endlessly poured out food gave its name directly to any overflowing abundant supply.

corollary.literal: a small garland, a bonus gift
corollary.path: In Latin a corollarium was the extra garland or tip given beyond what was owed, a gratuity. That sense of 'something extra that comes with the main thing' shifted to a logical consequence that follows naturally from a prior result.

corporeal.path: Directly from Latin corpus, 'body.' Corporeal simply means having a physical body, as opposed to spiritual or abstract.

corpulent.path: Latin corpulentus meant literally 'full-bodied.' It settled into describing someone whose body is very full indeed: fat, bulky.

correlate.literal: brought back together, related to each other
correlate.path: Built from the same root as 'relate.' To correlate is for two things to be carried back to one another, shown to rise and fall together.

corroborate.path: From robur, 'oak, strength.' To corroborate a claim is to add oak-solid strength to it with supporting evidence.

corrosion.path: Rust and acid are pictured gnawing at metal the way an animal gnaws a bone, wearing it away bit by bit.

cosmopolitan.path: A cosmopolitan person belongs to no single city or country but claims the whole world as home, comfortable across cultures.

cosset.literal: a pet lamb raised by hand
cosset.path: A cosset was originally a lamb kept as a household pet and hand-fed rather than left in the field. The verb kept that image: to cosset someone is to fuss over and indulge them the way a hand-raised lamb was doted on. The word's ultimate origin is uncertain.

cosseted.literal: treated like a hand-raised pet lamb
cosseted.path: Same word as 'cosset': someone cosseted has been fussed over and shielded from hardship like a lamb kept as a household pet. Origin uncertain.

coterie.path: In medieval France a coterie was a band of peasants jointly holding a cottage-plot from a lord. The word narrowed to any small, closed circle of associates who keep to themselves.

coterminous.path: Two things that are coterminous have their end-lines lined up exactly together, whether in territory or in time.

countenance.path: Countenance originally meant one's facial bearing or demeanor. To countenance an act is to show it a favorable face, that is, to approve or tolerate it.

counterintuitive.literal: against what is looked upon as obvious
counterintuitive.path: Intuition is what seems obviously true at a glance. Something counterintuitive runs directly against that first-glance judgment.

countermand.path: A countermand is a new order issued directly against an earlier one, canceling it.

counterpoint.path: From medieval music theory, 'note set against note': one melodic line placed against another. The word widened to any contrasting element set against another to bring it out.

counterproductive.path: Something counterproductive works directly against the very output it was meant to produce.

court.literal: the enclosed yard of a king's retinue
court.path: A royal court was the enclosed household where nobles gathered to win the ruler's favor. To 'court' someone keeps that image: paying the same kind of studied attention to win them over, or, by extension, inviting risk the way one might invite a rival's attention.

covert.path: Past participle of Old French covrir, 'to cover.' Something covert is kept fully covered from view, hidden from open sight.

covet.path: From the same root as cupidity and Cupid. To covet is to feel that same burning desire, but aimed at something that belongs to someone else.

cow.path: Probably from an Old Norse word for oppressing or subduing; unrelated to the barnyard animal. To cow someone is to browbeat them into submission.

cower.path: Probably from a Scandinavian word for crouching or lying low. To cower is to shrink low to the ground, the posture of fear.

coy.path: Old French coi meant simply quiet or still. That stillness narrowed first to modest reserve, then to a deliberately playful, evasive show of shyness.

cozen.path: Origin disputed: perhaps from French cousiner, to claim kinship in order to exploit someone's hospitality, or from an Italian word for shady horse-trading. Either story points to gaining someone's trust falsely in order to cheat them.

crabbed.path: Named for the crab's sideways, snapping movements: a crabbed temper is sour and irritable, and crabbed handwriting crawls crookedly across the page the way a crab scuttles sideways.

craft.path: Old English cræft meant raw strength or power before it narrowed to skill and then to cunning: the sense that skillful ability can shade into sly manipulation.

crafty.path: Built on 'craft.' Skillful ability shaded into cunning: a crafty person is skilled at getting their way, often through deception.

craven.path: Old French cravanté meant utterly crushed or defeated in battle. A soldier so broken came to stand for cowardice itself: craven describes contemptible, defeated-before-they-start fear.

credence.path: Directly from credere, 'to believe.' To give credence to something is to grant it belief.

credibility.path: From credere. Credibility is the quality of being worthy of belief.

credible.path: Straightforward from credere: something credible can be believed.

creditable.path: From the same root as 'credit.' A creditable effort is one that earns credit, that is, mild praise for being solidly done.

credo.path: The Latin opening word of the Christian creed, 'I believe,' generalized to mean any statement of one's core beliefs or principles.

credulity.path: From credere, 'to believe,' with a suffix for 'easily inclined to.' Credulity is a readiness to believe that outruns the evidence.

credulous.path: Same root as credulity: a credulous person believes too readily, without demanding real proof.

crescendo.path: Italian musical term, present participle of 'to grow.' A crescendo is a passage that keeps growing louder until it peaks.

crestfallen.path: Pictures a rooster whose comb droops after losing a fight, the visible sign of a beaten spirit. Applied to people, it means visibly deflated by disappointment.

crevice.path: From the same Latin verb for cracking or breaking that gives 'decrepit' and 'craven.' A crevice is simply a narrow crack or split opening.

crew.path: A crew originally meant a body of fresh troops sent to reinforce an army, an 'increase' in numbers. It settled into meaning any organized team working together, especially aboard a ship.

crone.path: Originally an insult for a worn-out old ewe, literally an old carcass, later applied to a withered old woman, especially as a folklore figure.

croon.path: A Germanic imitative word for a low murmuring sound, originally a lament. It softened into singing softly and sentimentally.

cryptic.path: Straight from Greek kryptos, 'hidden.' Something cryptic has a meaning deliberately buried out of easy sight.

crystallize.literal: to turn to ice, to form crystal
crystallize.path: Water freezing into crystal gives the image: a vague idea that crystallizes is pictured hardening into a clear, fixed shape.

culminate.path: From culmen, 'the topmost point.' Events that culminate are pictured climbing to their highest point before resolving.

culpability.path: Straight from culpa, 'fault.' Culpability is simply the state of deserving blame for a fault.
